parts.label: (a)

markscheme_points.text: potential difference applied between the plates
causes charge separation (between the plates) or causes energy to be stored (between the plates)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what a capacitor fundamentally needs - two conductors separated by an insulator. How do the metal plates and the air gap with insulating pads in Fig. 6.1 match this?
Hint 2: Now imagine connecting a battery across the two plates. What happens to charge on each plate, and what is then stored between them?
parts.proper_answer: Applying a p.d. between the plates causes equal and opposite charges to build up on the plates (charge separation). Energy is then stored in the electric field between the plates.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the capacitor structure**
You have two good conductors, the flat metal plates, facing each other with a small gap. The gap is air plus insulating pads, so there is no conducting path between them. That is exactly a parallel-plate capacitor: conductor - insulator - conductor.

Step 2: **Connect a p.d. to store charge and energy**
If you apply a potential difference across the plates, one plate becomes positive and the other becomes negative with equal magnitude of charge. Charge is separated and held apart, so $$Q = C V$$. Work is done to do this, so energy is stored in the electric field between the plates.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The arrangement in Fig. 6.1 has capacitance $C$. The arrangement is connected into the circuit of Fig. 6.2.

{{figure:figure_6_2}}

When the two-way switch is moved to position A, the capacitor is charged so that the potential difference across it is $V$. When the switch moves to position B, the capacitor fully discharges through the sensitive ammeter.

The switch moves repeatedly between A and B so that the capacitor charges and then discharges with frequency $f$.
parts.text:
Show that the average current $I$ in the ammeter is given by

$$I = CVf.$$

markscheme_points.text: clear substitution of $Q = CV$ and $f = 1 / t$, leading

hints: Hint 1: Start from what average current always means - charge flowing per unit time. In this circuit, what packet of charge flows through the ammeter each time the capacitor discharges?
Hint 2: Link that packet of charge to $C$ and $V$, and link the time between discharges to the switching frequency $f$. How can you combine them to eliminate $Q$ and $t$?
parts.proper_answer: Average current $I = Q/t$ where $Q = CV$ is charge per discharge and $t = 1/f$ is time per cycle. So $I = CV/(1/f) = CVf$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write down average current**
Current is rate of flow of charge. For repeated pulses, the average over many cycles is total charge divided by total time, which is the same as charge per cycle divided by time per cycle: $$I = \frac{Q}{t}$$ Here $Q$ is the charge that flows through the ammeter in one full discharge.

Step 2: **Substitute Q and t**
From the definition of capacitance, the charge stored when charged to $V$ is: $$Q = C V$$ The switch charges then discharges with frequency $f$, so the time for one charge-discharge cycle is the period: $$t = \frac{1}{f}$$ Putting them into $I = Q/t$ gives: $$I = \frac{CV}{1/f} = CVf$$ That is the average discharge current read by the sensitive ammeter.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
For a potential difference $V$ of $180\text{ V}$ and a frequency $f$ of switching of $50\text{ Hz}$, the average current $I$ in the ammeter is $2.5\ \mu\text{A}$.

Calculate the capacitance, in $\text{pF}$, of the parallel plates.
hints: Hint 1: You have just shown $I = CVf$. Look at which three quantities are given and which one you need. How will you isolate the capacitance $C$ before putting numbers in?
Hint 2: Check your units carefully - convert $2.5 \, \mu\text{A}$ to amps, calculate $C$ in farads, then convert to pF using $1 \, \text{pF} = 10^{-12} \, \text{F}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Rearrange for C**
You know $I$, $V$ and $f$, so make $C$ the subject: $$I = CVf$$ $$C = \frac{I}{Vf}$$

Step 2: **Substitute and convert to pF**
Convert current: $$I = 2.5 \, \mu\text{A} = 2.5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A}$$ Then: $$C = \frac{2.5 \times 10^{-6}}{180 \times 50} = 2.78 \times 10^{-10} \text{ F}$$ Since $1 \, \text{pF} = 10^{-12} \text{ F}$: $$C = \frac{2.78 \times 10^{-10}}{10^{-12}} \approx 280 \text{ pF}$$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A second capacitor is connected into the circuit of Fig. 6.2. The two capacitors are connected in parallel.

State and explain the change, if any, in the average current in the ammeter.

markscheme_points.text: greater charge (for each cycle/discharge) so greater (average) current or $V$ and $f$ are constant so (average) current increases or $I$ is (directly) proportional to $C$ so (average) current increases

hints: Hint 1: Recall the rule for combining capacitors in parallel. Does the total capacitance increase, decrease or stay the same when you add a second capacitor alongside the first?
Hint 2: Use $I = CVf$ with $V$ and $f$ unchanged. If total $C$ changes, what must happen to the charge moved per cycle and hence to the average current?
parts.proper_answer: Total capacitance increases. For the same $V$ and $f$, greater charge is stored and discharged each cycle, so average current $I = CVf$ increases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the new total capacitance**
In parallel, capacitances add: $$C_{total} = C_1 + C_2$$ So adding a second capacitor in parallel always increases the total capacitance that is charged to $V$ each time.

Step 2: **Link to average current**
From part (b)(i), $$I = C_{total}Vf$$ Both the charging voltage $V$ and the switching frequency $f$ are unchanged. Since $I$ is directly proportional to $C$, a larger $C_{total}$ means more charge $Q = CV$ flows per discharge, so the average current in the ammeter increases.

key_concepts: proportionality of average current to capacitance
